readings.c1s3:
¶
'''word-deafness''' (wėrd′def″nes), ''n.'' Loss, through disease, of the ability to understand spoken language, although the sounds are heard and the faculties of reading and speaking may be unimpaired.

'''worder''' (wėr′dėr), ''n.'' [< ''word''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] A speaker. ''Whitlock.'' [Rare.]

'''wordily''' (wėr′di-li), ''adv.'' In a verbose or wordy manner.

'''wordiness''' (wėr′di-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being wordy or of abounding with words.

'''wording''' (wėr′ding), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''word''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' The style or manner in which something is expressed; the form of words used in expressing some thought, idea, or the like; diction; phraseology.
{{smaller block|It is believed the ''wording'' was above his known style and orthography.
{{right|''Milton.''}}}}
'''2.''' Expression, or power of expression; language; words.
{{smaller block|Things for which no ''wording'' can be found.
{{right|''Keats'', Endymion, iv.}}}}

'''wordish†''' (wėr′dish), ''a.'' [< ''word''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] Verbal; wordy.
{{smaller block|An image of that whereof the Philosopher bestoweth but a ''woordish'' description.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Apol. for Poetrie (ed. Arber), p. 33.}}}}

'''wordishness†''' (wėr′dish-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' The state or quality of being wordish.—'''2.''' Verbosity; prolixity.
readings.c2s1:
{{smaller block|The truth they hide by their dark ''wordishness.''
{{right|''Sir K. Digby'', Bodies, Prefatory Verses.}}}}

¶
'''wordle''' (wėr′dl), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] One of the pivoted adjustable cams which form the throat of a drawhead-die through which wire or lead pipe is drawn. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''wordless''' (wėrd′les), ''a.'' [< ME. ''wordles'' (= Icel. ''orthlauss, orthalauss''); < ''word''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.''] '''1.''' Silent; speechless.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wordlesse'' he was, and semede sicke.</poem>
{{right|''Isle of Ladies'', l. 516.}}
<poem>Her joy with heaved-up hand she doth express,
And, ''wordless'', so greets heaven for his success.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 112.}}}}
'''2.''' Unexpressed in words.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wordlesse'' answere in no toun
Was tane for obligatioun,
Ne called surety in no wise.</poem>
{{right|''Isle of Ladies'', l. 889.}}
Silent people often get insane. It is not safe to have too many dealings with ''wordless'' thoughts.
{{right|''Noctes Ambrosianæ'', April, 1832.}}}}

'''word-memory''' (wėrd′mem″ō-ri), ''n.'' The memory of words; the power of recalling words to the mind.

'''word-painter''' (wėrd′pān″tėr), ''n.'' A writer who has the power of graphic or vivid description in depicting scenes or events; one who displays picturesqueness of style.

'''word-painting''' (wėrd′pān″ting), ''n.'' The act of describing or depicting in words graphically or vividly.

'''word-picture''' (wėrd′pik″t̮ūr), ''n.'' A graphic or vivid description of any scene or event, so that it is presented to the mind as in a picture.

'''wordsman†''' (wėrdz′ma̤n), ''n.'' [< ''words'', pl. of ''word''<sup>1</sup>, + ''man''.] One who attaches undue importance to words, or who deals in mere words; one skilled in the use of words; a verbalist. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Some speculative ''wordsman.''{{right|''Bushnell.''}}}}

'''wordsmanship†''' (wėrdz′ma̤n-ship), ''n.'' [< ''wordsman'' + ''-ship''.] Knowledge or command of words; fluency in speech or writing.

'''word-spite†''' (wėrd′spīt), ''a.'' Expressing spite; abusive.
{{smaller block|A silly, yet ferocious, ''wordspite'' quarrel between Otho and Hugh-le-Grand.{{right|''Sir F. Palgrave'', Norm. and Eng., II. 561.}}}}

'''word-square''' (wėrd′skwãr), ''n.'' See ''square''<sup>1</sup>, 15.

'''wordstrife''' (wėrd′strīf), ''n.'' Disputing about words; logomachy. ''Bp. Hacket'', Abp. Williams, ii. 107. (''Davies.'')

'''word<sup>1</sup>''' (wėrd), ''v.''   [< ME. ''worden'', ''wordien''; < ''word''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To express in words; phrase.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Word'' it
In the most generous terms.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Magnetick Lady, iii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|The apology for the king is the same, but ''worded'' with greater deference to that great prince.
{{right|''Addison.''}}}}
'''2.''' To ply with or overpower by words; talk.
{{smaller block|If one were to be ''worded'' to Death, Italian is the fittest Language, in regard of the Fluency and Softness of it.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. i. 42.}}}}
'''3†.''' To flatter; cajole.
{{smaller block|<poem>He ''words'' me, girls, he ''words'' me, that I should not
Be noble to myself.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., v. 2. 191.}}}}
'''4.''' To make or unmake by a word or command. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Against him . . . who could ''word'' heaven and earth out of nothing, and can when he pleases ''word'' them into nothing again.
{{right|''South'', Sermons, X. v.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To speak; talk; converse; discourse.
{{smaller block|<poem>And tho that wisely ''wordeden'' and wryten many bokes
Of witte and of wisdome with dampned soules wonye.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), x. 428.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus ''wording'' timidly among the fierce:
“O Father! I am here the simplest voice.”</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Hyperion, ii.}}}}
'''To word it''', {{smaller|to wrangle; dispute; contend in words.}}
{{smaller block|He that descends not to ''word it'' with a shrew does worse than beat her.
{{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange.''}}}}

'''word<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' An erroneous form of ''ord.''

'''word-blind''' (wėrd′blīnd), ''a.'' Deprived of the visual memory of the signs of language. {{smaller|Unable, as a result of disease, to read, though possibly retaining the ability to speak, write, and understand spoken words.}}
{{smaller block|M. de Capdeville noted the curious fact that ''word-blind'' persons are sometimes able to read manuscript but not print.
{{right|''Proc. Soc. Psych. Research'', III. 48.}}}}

'''word-blindness''' (wėrd′blīnd″nes), ''n.'' Loss, through disease, of the ability to read, although the faculties of speaking, writing, and understanding spoken words may remain unimpaired.

'''word-book''' (wėrd′bu̇k), ''n.''   [< ''word''<sup>1</sup> + ''book''; after D. ''woordenboek'' = G. ''wörterbuch'' = Icel. ''ortha-bók'' = Sw. ''ordbok'' = Dan. ''ordbog''.]   A book containing words with their explanations, arranged in alphabetical or other regular order; a vocabulary; a dictionary; a lexicon.
{{smaller block|If no other bookes can be so vvell perfected, but still some thing may be added, hovv much less a ''Word-booke?''
{{right|''Florio'', It. Dict. (1598), To the Reader, p. [13].}}}}

'''word-bound''' (wėrd′bound), ''a.'' Restrained or restricted in speech; unable or unwilling to express one’s self; also, bound by one’s word or promise.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Word-bound'' he is not;
He’ll tell it willingly.</poem>
{{right|''J. Baillie.''}}}}

'''word-building''' (wėrd′bil″ding), ''n.'' The formation, construction, or composition of words.

'''word-catcher''' (wėrd′kach″ėr), ''n.'' One who cavils at words.
{{smaller block|Each ''word-catcher'', that lives on syllables.
{{right|''Pope'', Prol. to Satires, l. 166.}}}}

{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Apol. for Poetrie (ed. Arber), p. 33.}}}}

{{right|''Sir K. Digby'', Bodies, Prefatory Verses.}}}}

'''wordless''' (wėrd′les), ''a.''   [< ME. ''wordles'' (= Icel. ''orthlauss, orthalauss''); < ''word''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.'']   '''1.''' Silent; speechless.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wordlesse'' he was, and semede sicke.</poem>
{{right|''Isle of Ladies'', l. 516.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Her joy with heaved-up hand she doth express,
And, ''wordless'', so greets heaven for his success.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 112.}}}}
'''2.''' Unexpressed in words.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wordlesse'' answere in no toun
Was tane for obligatioun,
Ne called surety in no wise.</poem>
{{right|''Isle of Ladies'', l. 889.}}}}
{{smaller block|Silent people often get insane. It is not safe to have too many dealings with ''wordless'' thoughts.
{{right|''Noctes Ambrosianæ'', April, 1832.}}}}

'''word-painting''' (wėrd′pān″ting), ''n.'' The act of describing or depicting in words graphically or vividly.

'''word-picture''' (wėrd′pik″t̮ūr), ''n.'' A graphic or vivid description of any scene or event, so that it is presented to the mind as in a picture.

'''wordsman†''' (wėrdz′ma̤n), ''n.''   [< ''words'', pl. of ''word''<sup>1</sup>, + ''man''.]   One who attaches undue importance to words, or who deals in mere words; one skilled in the use of words; a verbalist. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Some speculative ''wordsman.''{{right|''Bushnell.''}}}}

'''wordsmanship†''' (wėrdz′ma̤n-ship), ''n.''   [< ''wordsman'' + ''-ship''.]   Knowledge or command of words; fluency in speech or writing.

'''word-spite†''' (wėrd′spīt), ''a.'' Expressing spite; abusive.
{{smaller block|A silly, yet ferocious, ''wordspite'' quarrel between Otho and Hugh-le-Grand.{{right|''Sir F. Palgrave'', Norm. and Eng., II. 561.}}}}

'''word-square''' (wėrd′skwãr), ''n.'' See ''square''<sup>1</sup>, 15.

'''wordstrife''' (wėrd′strīf), ''n.'' Disputing about words; logomachy.   ''Bp. Hacket'', Abp. Williams, ii. 107. (''Davies.'')

'''Wordsworthian''' (wėrdz′wėr-thi-an), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ''Wordsworth'' (see def.) + ''-ian.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to the English poet William Wordsworth (1770–1850), or to his style.

'''II.''' ''n.'' An admirer or a follower of the poet Wordsworth.
{{smaller block|The ''Wordsworthians'' were a sect who, if they had the enthusiasm, had also not a little of the exclusiveness and partiality to which sects are liable.
{{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 201.}}}}

'''Wordsworth’s flower.''' See ''Ranunculus.''

'''wordy<sup>1</sup>''' (wėr′di), ''a.''   [< ME. ''woordy'' (= Icel. ''orthigr''); < ''word''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Given to the use of many words; verbose.
{{smaller block|A ''wordy'' orator . . . making a magnificent speech to the people, full of vain promises. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 448.}}}}
'''2.''' Full of words; wordish.
{{smaller block|We need not lavish hours in ''wordy'' periods.
{{right|''Philips'', The Briton.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''wordy'' variance of domestic life;
The tyrant husband, the retorting wife.</poem>
{{right|''Crabbe'', Works, I. 159.}}}}
'''3.''' Consisting of words; verbal.
{{smaller block|A silent, but amused spectator of this ''wordy'' combat.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Shirley, iv.}}}}

'''wordy<sup>2</sup>†''', ''a.'' An obsolete Scotch form of ''worthy.''

'''wore<sup>1</sup>''' (wōr). Preterit of ''wear''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wore<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v.'' An obsolete variant of ''were.'' See ''was.''

'''wore<sup>3</sup>†''', ''v. t.''   [ME. ''woren'', < AS. ''wōrian'', weary, fatigue, wander.]   To weary; fatigue. See ''weary''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.''   ''Ancren Riwle'', p. 386.

'''woreld†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''world.''

'''work''' (wėrk), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''worked'' or ''wrought'', ppr. ''working.''   [< ME. ''worken'', ''werken'', ''wirken'', also assibilated ''worchen'', ''wurchen'', ''werchen'', ''warchen'', ''wirchen'' (pret. ''wrouhte'', ''wrouȝte'', ''wroute'', ''wrohte'', ''worhte'', pp. ''wrought'', ''wrouȝt'', ''wroght'', ''wroȝt'', ''wroht''), < AS. ''wyrcan'', ''wircan'', ''wercan'' (pret. ''worhte'', pp. ''geworht'') = OS. ''wirkean'' = OFries. ''werka'', ''wirtsa'' = D. ''werken'' = MLG. ''werken'', ''worken'', LG. ''werken'' = OHG. ''wirchen'', ''wurchen'', MHG. ''wirken'', ''würken'', G. ''wirken'' = Icel. ''yrkja'' (for ''vyrkja'') = Dan. ''virke'' = Goth. ''waurkjan'', work; a secondary verb, associated with the noun ''work'', from a Teut. √ ''werk'', √ ''work'', = Gr. *ἔργειν, perf. ἔοργα, work, ῥέζειν (for *Ϝρέγjειν), do (cf. ἔργον, a work, ὄργανον, instrument, organ), = Zend √ ''vrz'', ''verez'', work; cf. Pers. ''warz'', gain, profit, habit, etc. From the Gr. words of this root are ult. E. ''erg'', ''energy'', ''organ'', etc., and the second element in ''metallurgy'', ''theurgy'', etc., ''chirurgeon'', ''surgeon'', etc.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To put forth effort for the accomplishment of something; exert one’s self in the performance of some service; labor; toil; strive: as, to ''work'' ten hours a day.
{{smaller block|<poem>But whi the werwolf so ''wrouȝt'' wondred thei alle,
& whi more with the king than with any other.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4035.}}}}
{{smaller block|We commanded you that, if any would not ''work'', neither should he eat.
{{right|2 Thes. iii. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>My sweet mistress
Weeps when she sees me ''work'', and says such baseness
Had never like executor.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iii. 1. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|His labor more than requited his entertainment; for he ''wrought'' among us with vigor, and either in the meadow or at the hay-rick put himself foremost.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, viii.}}}}

'''2.''' To act; operate; carry on or perform a function; operate effectively; prove practicable: as, the pump will not ''work;'' a plan or system that ''works'' well; the charm ''works''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Louse thi lippes a-twynne & let the gost ''worche''.</poem>
{{right|''Joseph of Arimathie'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Nature hath now no dominacioun:
And certeynly ther nature wol nat ''wirche''.
Farewel, phisyk! go ber the man to chirche.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 1901.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But once the circle got within,
The charms to ''work'' do straight begin,
And he was caught as in a gin.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Nymphidia.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Soon as the potion ''works'', their human countenance,
The express resemblance of the gods, is changed.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 68.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Love never fails to master what he finds,
But ''works'' a different way in different minds.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Cym. and Iph., l. 465.}}}}
{{smaller block|You may make everything else out of the passions of men except a political system that will ''work''.
{{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 158.}}}}
'''3.''' To ferment, as liquors.
{{smaller block|This experiment would be transferred unto other wine and strong beer by putting in some like substances while they ''work''.
{{right|''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 782.}}}}
'''4.''' To be agitated or in a state of restless movement or commotion; seethe; toss; rage.
{{smaller block|<poem>Calm is the sea; the waues ''worke'' lesse and lesse.</poem>
{{right|''Surrey'', Complaint by Night of Louer Not Beloued.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The dog-star foams, and the stream boils,
And curls, and ''works'', and swells ready to sparkle.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sad Shepherd, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|The inward wretchedness of his wicked heart, he says, began to be discovered to him, and to ''work'' as it had never done before; he was now conscious of sinful thoughts and desires which he had not till then regarded.
{{right|''Southey'', Bunyan, p. 22.}}}}
'''5.''' To make way laboriously and slowly; make progress, become, or get with exertion and difficulty: generally followed by an adjective, or by an adverb of direction, as ''along'', ''down'', ''into'', ''out'', ''through'', ''up'', etc.: as, to ''work loose''; to ''work out''; to ''work up''. {{smaller block|<poem>Who would trust chance, since all men have the seeds
Of good and ill, which should ''work upward'' first?</poem>
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
{{smaller block|After midnight . . . the wind ''worked'' gradually round . . . and blew directly in our teeth.
{{right|''Lady Brassey'', Voyage of Sunbeam, I. i.}}}}
'''6.''' To carry on systematic operations in some department of human activity, especially as a means of earning a livelihood; be regularly engaged or employed in some operation, trade, profession, or business: as, to ''work'' in brass or iron.
{{smaller block|They that ''work'' in fine flax . . . shall be confounded.
{{right|Isa. xix. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Sea-faring men, who long have ''wrought''
In the great deep for gain. ''M. Arnold'', Balder Dead.</poem>}}
'''7.''' To do something; specifically, to be employed in handiwork, as in knitting, sewing, or embroidery.
{{smaller block|“I always think it is such a waste of time to sit out of doors or listen to reading without ''working''.” “But I can’t ''work'',” said Archie, “except mending, and that I detest.”
{{right|''Mrs. Annie Edwards'', Archie Lovell, xxx.}}}}
'''8.''' To blossom, as water; become full of some vegetable substance. See the quotation.
{{smaller block|Nearly all the ponds, rivers, and lakes ''work'', or what is generally called “blossom,” some waters once and some twice during the summer months. A vegetable substance that grows on the bottom, and during the summer the seed or bloom, breaks loose from the bottom and floats in the water. The leaves of the blossoms are of the same weight as the water, so that some kinds do not come to the top and float, but float about in the water, giving the water a thick oily appearance. Very few fish are caught when the water is in blossom.
{{right|''Seth Green.''}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
